content: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a complex medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure in the arteries of the lungs, leading to strain on the right side of the heart. PH can result from various causes including lung diseases, left heart disease, chronic blood clots, or diseases affecting blood vessels in the lungs. The underlying pathophysiology involves narrowing, remodeling, or obstruction of pulmonary arteries, increasing pulmonary vascular resistance and right ventricular workload. Symptoms commonly include shortness of breath (dyspnea), fatigue, chest discomfort, and swelling in the legs. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical assessment and diagnostic tests such as echocardiography, right heart catheterization, chest imaging, and pulmonary function tests. Treatment strategies vary based on the PH type and cause but often incorporate vasodilator medications, oxygen therapy, anticoagulation, and in selected cases, surgical interventions like pulmonary thromboendarterectomy or lung transplantation. Lifestyle modifications, including avoidance of high altitudes and strenuous exertion, smoking cessation, and nutritional support, play a crucial supportive role. Major synonyms include pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), though PAH specifically refers to Group 1 PH according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification. Evidence for treatment efficacy is strongest for PAH medications such as endothelin receptor antagonists and phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors, while treatment for other PH groups relies more heavily on addressing underlying causes. Limitations exist due to the heterogeneity of PH, complexity of diagnosis, and potential side effects of therapies. Safety considerations emphasize regular monitoring for medication adverse effects, recognition of symptom worsening, and addressing comorbidities. This module provides comprehensive information ensuring independent understandability of each topic for effective retrieval and patient education.

chunk_title: Definition and Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension
content: Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) is defined by an increase in mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) ≥20 mmHg at rest, measured by right heart catheterization, the gold standard diagnostic test. The World Health Organization classifies PH into five groups based on etiology: Group 1 - Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), Group 2 - PH due to left heart disease, Group 3 - PH due to lung diseases and/or hypoxia, Group 4 - chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), and Group 5 - PH with unclear or multifactorial mechanisms. This classification aids in targeted diagnosis and management.

chunk_title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Pulmonary Hypertension
content: PH arises from increased pulmonary vascular resistance due to vasoconstriction, remodeling of pulmonary arteries (including smooth muscle hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis), thrombosis, or obstruction. These changes elevate pulmonary arterial pressures, causing right ventricular hypertrophy and potentially right heart failure. Molecular pathways involved include endothelial dysfunction, imbalance of vasodilators (e.g., nitric oxide, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (e.g., endothelin-1), inflammation, and genetic factors affecting vascular cell proliferation.

content: PH can result from multiple underlying conditions. Risk factors include connective tissue diseases (e.g., scleroderma), congenital heart diseases, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), interstitial lung disease, left heart failure, recurrent pulmonary emboli, sickle cell disease, portal hypertension, and certain medications/toxins like appetite suppressants. Genetic predispositions exist especially in heritable PAH.

content: Patients with PH commonly experience progressive dyspnea (shortness of breath) on exertion, fatigue, chest pain or discomfort, palpitations, syncope (fainting), and peripheral edema (swelling of legs). Signs include loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, jugular venous distension, and sometimes cyanosis. Symptom severity often correlates with PH progression and right ventricular compromise.

content: Diagnosis involves clinical assessment and supportive testing: echocardiography estimates pulmonary artery pressure and right heart function. Right heart catheterization confirms diagnosis and measures hemodynamics. Additional evaluations include chest X-ray, CT scan for lung assessment, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan to assess for thromboembolic disease, pulmonary function tests, blood tests to detect associated conditions, and ECG to detect right heart strain.

content: Treatment is tailored to PH type and underlying cause. PAH-specific therapies include endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan), phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil), prostacyclin analogs, and soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators. Oxygen therapy may be required for hypoxemic patients. Anticoagulation is standard for CTEPH unless contraindicated. Diuretics help manage right heart failure symptoms. Experimental therapies and lung transplantation are options for refractory cases.

content: Lifestyle modifications support PH management: physical activity should be moderate and individualized, avoiding high-intensity exertion; smoking cessation is critical; altitude exposure should be minimized due to hypoxia risk. Nutritional support and psychosocial counseling improve quality of life. Regular medical follow-up and vaccination against respiratory infections are recommended to prevent complications.

content: PH can lead to progressive right ventricular failure, arrhythmias, and sudden death. Prognosis depends on PH etiology, response to therapy, and right heart function. Early diagnosis and treatment improve survival. Some types, like idiopathic PAH, have a guarded prognosis while PH due to left heart disease depends on cardiac management outcomes.

content: Misconceptions include: PH is the same as systemic hypertension (they are different — PH affects lungs); PAH only affects older adults (it can affect all ages including children); No effective treatments exist (several medications have proven benefits); All patients should avoid all exercise (individualized activity is beneficial). Addressing myths helps patients engage in appropriate care.

content: Regular monitoring includes periodic echocardiograms and clinical assessments for symptom progression or medication side effects such as liver toxicity or low blood pressure. Patients should report worsening symptoms promptly. Some PH medications have teratogenic risks, making pregnancy counseling essential. Immunizations and infection prevention are critical due to increased vulnerability.
